cases.title: Restoring inherited paint-server transforms in usvg
cases.original_title: fix(usvg): inherit `gradientTransform` and `patternTransform` via `href`
cases.role: Pull request author · tests added by maintainer

sections.heading: The problem
sections.text: In usvg's paint_server.rs, convert_linear, convert_radial and convert_pattern read their transform with node.resolve_transform, which ignores the href template chain. A template's gradientTransform or patternTransform was therefore dropped, as diagnosed in #1134.

sections.heading: Why it was needed
sections.text: According to the report, the regression had shipped since v0.37.0 and remained in v0.48.1. Any fix had to restore inheritance without undoing the transform-origin support whose introduction caused the loss.

sections.heading: My contribution and the accepted change
sections.text: My commit changes three call sites to resolve_attr(node, ...).resolve_transform(...), so the element that defines the transform is found first and transform-origin is read from that same element. After luisbg said the fix looked good but asked for a regression test, LaurenzV added a commit with linear, radial and pattern via-href cases covering direct, inherited, chained and overridden use.

sections.heading: Why this approach
sections.text: Implementation-derived rationale: reusing the existing resolve_attr helper revives the GradientTransform entries already present in resolve_lg_attr and resolve_rg_attr instead of adding lookup code, and a transform on the element itself still takes precedence. The PR description documents both properties.

sections.heading: Validation and outcome
sections.text: Author-reported: the reproducer passes, output matches rsvg-convert 2.58 within 1/255 per channel, and cargo test passed 1731 integration tests with no reference-image changes, on Linux only. My local paired tests were not submitted; the merged tests are LaurenzV's. LaurenzV squash-merged the PR on October 3, 2026.

cases.title: Tracing lost gradient transforms to a regression
cases.original_title: `gradientTransform` and `patternTransform` are not inherited through `href`
cases.role: Bug reporter · regression analysis and merged fix

sections.heading: The problem
sections.text: A gradient or pattern using another as a template through href inherited stops, coordinates, units and spreadMethod, but not gradientTransform or patternTransform. In my minimal SVG, a gold-to-navy gradient whose template is rotated 90 degrees rendered left to right in resvg instead of top to bottom.

sections.heading: Why it was needed
sections.text: SVG 2 explicitly lists these transforms among the attributes copied from a template, and SVG 1.1 states the rule generally. The report showed the same loss for a radial gradient translation and a rotated pattern, so documents that reuse paint servers could render incorrectly.

sections.heading: My contribution and the resolution
sections.text: I traced the cause to 9101f30a, the transform-origin change first released in v0.37.0: resolve_transform reads only the element itself, leaving the href-aware GradientTransform lookups unused. I proposed resolving the defining element first, attached before/after renders compared with rsvg-convert, and opened #1135, whose merge on October 3, 2026 closed the issue.

sections.heading: Why this approach
sections.text: Rather than patching the symptom, the report compared the v0.36.0 converters with the current ones and noted that no existing attributes-via-xlink-href test set a transform on the referenced element, explaining why the regression went unnoticed. The proposal keeps transform-origin support and lets a local transform win.

sections.heading: Validation and outcome
sections.text: My pixel comparisons (within 1/255 after the fix, up to 255 before) are author-reported. Independently, matthargett commented that a new WPT reftest covers this case, that usvg 0.48.1 renders it untransformed, and that Chromium 131 and Firefox agree on the expected output. LaurenzV closed the issue on 2026-10-03.

cases.title: Restoring the cylinder containment test
cases.original_title: Fix cylinder point containment

sections.heading: The problem
sections.text: CylinderClass::containsPoint, the cylinder implementation behind Shape::containsPoint, evaluated its radial term as point.x * point.x + point.y + point.y. For cylinderShape(1, 2) the interior point (0, 0.75, 0) was rejected and the exterior point (0, -2, 0) was accepted.

sections.heading: Why it was needed
sections.text: Containment should be symmetric about the cylinder's Z axis. Adding Y twice instead of squaring it made the answer depend on the sign of Y and accepted arbitrarily negative Y when X and Z were zero, so the error was not confined to boundary points. Companion report #29 documents the standalone reproducer.

sections.heading: My contribution and the accepted change
sections.text: The accepted change is one line in Physics3D/geometry/builtinShapeClasses.cpp: y + y becomes y * y, so the radial check reads x*x + y*y <= 1.0 beside the unchanged abs(z) <= 1.0 cap test. No other file, signature or shape class changed. The PR was opened about a minute before I filed #29, and its body links that issue with Fixes #29.

sections.heading: Why this approach
sections.text: Documented: the PR frames the defect as broken cylinder symmetry and restores the squared term. Implementation-derived: correcting the shared shape-class predicate fixes every containsPoint caller for cylinders at once, without touching the separate intersection-distance code below it in the same file.

sections.heading: Validation and outcome
sections.text: Author-reported: a Debug build with GCC 16.0.1 passed all 13 geometry tests, and a local 30-assertion regression test over both signs of X and Y, two radii, and radial and cap boundaries failed before the fix and passed after. That test is quoted in the PR body but was not committed, and the full suite was not run. VonTum replied "Oh, you are correct. Well spotted." and merged the PR on September 21, 2026.

cases.title: Reporting inverted cylinder containment
cases.original_title: Cylinder containsPoint rejects interior points and accepts exterior points
cases.role: Bug reporter · standalone reproducer and root cause

sections.heading: The problem
sections.text: Shape::containsPoint misclassified cylinders in both directions: for cylinderShape(1, 2), the point (0, 0.75, 0) returned false and (0, -2, 0) returned true. I confirmed this on commit 00691df with GCC 16.0.1, C++23 and a Debug build, using points away from the boundary.

sections.heading: Why it was needed
sections.text: A containment query that rejects interior points and accepts exterior ones is wrong for ordinary inputs, not only edge cases. I traced it to CylinderClass::containsPoint, where y + y stood in for y * y, and explained that the expression breaks radial symmetry and accepts arbitrarily negative Y when X and Z are zero.

sections.heading: My contribution and the resolution
sections.text: I supplied a short C++ program that links only the static physics library, the exact CMake and compiler commands, expected versus actual output, and a nonzero exit code as the pass/fail signal; no GUI or graphics dependencies are needed. On ordering: PR #28 was opened about a minute before this issue, which I filed as its companion report and pointed to #28 as the fix.

sections.heading: Why this approach
sections.text: Choosing an interior and an exterior point far from the boundary rules out tolerance arguments, and a self-contained program lets maintainers confirm the defect on unmodified source independently of the patch. That rationale is derived from the report's structure; the issue does not state it explicitly.

sections.heading: Validation and outcome
sections.text: The report states that the wrong results reproduced on original source and that, after the fix, all 13 geometry tests passed, including an uncommitted 30-assertion regression test; it also says the full suite was not run. These results are author-reported. VonTum confirmed the bug and merged #28 on September 21, 2026, and this issue closed with that merge.

cases.title: Parsing plus-signed float exponents in Flax
cases.original_title: Fix ParseFloat rejecting a '+' sign in the exponent

sections.heading: The problem
sections.text: ParseFloat folded exponent-sign handling into one ternary that advanced the cursor only for a minus. A plus sign stopped the digit loop immediately, and the trailing-character check returned failure before the result was stored, as reported in #4261.

sections.heading: Why it was needed
sections.text: A plus-signed exponent is the form printf's %g produces, as the reproducer's reference column shows. Because many callers ignore the return value, a stale output was indistinguishable from success. Fixing the shared template repairs both the char and wide Char instantiations at once.

sections.heading: My contribution and the accepted change
sections.text: Replaced the ternary with an explicit branch: a minus sets the multiplier to 0.1 and advances, a plus only advances, and the default stays 10. The accepted change is one commit with 10 additions and 1 deletion in StringUtilsBase.cpp. No test file was added.

sections.heading: Why this approach
sections.text: Implementation-derived rationale: leaving powerer at 10 makes e+N behave exactly like eN, while input without a plus takes the same path as before. The PR description states this equivalence; no review comments or alternative designs appear in the record.

sections.heading: Validation and outcome
sections.text: My harness extracted the before and after function bodies directly from git and compared them with strtod: 8/8 reported inputs fixed, 210 plus-free inputs, malformed ones included, bit-identical, and the wide Char path clean. These are author-reported results. Labeled core and fix under milestone 1.13, the PR was merged on September 14, 2026 by the flaxtechnology account; the merge commit is authored by Wojtek Figat.

cases.title: Keeping sprite offset setters independent
cases.original_title: Fix MainObject::setXOffset() overwriting the Y offset

sections.heading: The problem
sections.text: In is::Engine 4.0.x, MainObject::setXOffset() forwarded m_xOffset as the y argument to setXYOffset(). Because that helper assigns both members and calls updateSDMsprite(), changing the X offset also replaced the Y offset with the previous X value and moved the sprite, as reported in #9.

sections.heading: Why it was needed
sections.text: Offsets position an object’s sprite, and the header documents each setter as affecting one axis. Implementation-derived: until fixed, a caller wanting to change only X had to avoid setXOffset() and pass both values to setXYOffset() itself.

sections.heading: My contribution and the accepted change
sections.text: The accepted patch changes one argument in app/src/main/cpp/MainObject.cpp: setXYOffset(val, m_xOffset) becomes setXYOffset(val, m_yOffset). The commit message explains the overwrite and carries Fixes #9. No header, public API or other setter was modified.

sections.heading: Why this approach
sections.text: The corrected call mirrors setYOffset(), which already passed the untouched member for the other axis, so both setters share one pattern and still route through setXYOffset() and its sprite update. The PR explains that no test was added because the repository vendors catch.hpp but has no wired-up test suite or build target, and offers to upstream the harness.

sections.heading: Validation and outcome
sections.text: Author-reported: the translation unit compiled cleanly on the SFML backend with GCC and -std=c++17, and a local harness against the real class showed Y staying at 20 after the change instead of dropping to 10. The mirrored setYOffset() case passed before and after. No reviews or comments appear; Is-Daouda merged the PR into 4.0.x on September 14, 2026.

cases.title: Reporting an X setter that moved sprites vertically
cases.original_title: MainObject::setXOffset() overwrites the Y offset with the old X offset
cases.role: Bug reporter · reproducer and follow-up PR

sections.heading: The problem
sections.text: In is::Engine 4.0.3, calling MainObject::setXOffset() silently replaced the object’s Y offset with its previous X offset. Because the shared helper also refreshes the sprite, the visible symptom was a sprite shifting on the Y axis when only its X offset was changed.

sections.heading: Why it was needed
sections.text: The header documents the two setters as independent (Set the x offset / Set the y offset), and setYOffset() already honoured that, so the behaviour contradicted the documented contract rather than reflecting a design choice. Users had no signal beyond a misplaced sprite.

sections.heading: My contribution and the resolution
sections.text: I quoted setXOffset(), setYOffset() and setXYOffset() side by side, showing the old X value passed as the y argument, and gave a short reproducer: setXYOffset(10, 20) then setXOffset(5) leaves Y at 10 instead of 20. I named the version, branch and commit (4.0.3, 4.0.x, 46e75c8). The issue was resolved by my own PR #10.

sections.heading: Why this approach
sections.text: Placing the faulty setter next to its correct mirror let a maintainer confirm the bug by reading alone, without building the engine. The report separated expected from actual behaviour and noted that, although reproduced on SFML, the code path is backend-independent.

sections.heading: Validation and outcome
sections.text: Reproduction on the SFML backend under Linux, GCC and C++17 is author-reported. The report already proposed the one-line m_xOffset to m_yOffset fix and announced a PR. cases.title: Returning full-range angles between 3D vectors
cases.original_title: Fix VECTOR3D::GetAngle() returning the supplement for obtuse angles

sections.heading: The problem
sections.text: As diagnosed in #398, GetAngle computed only the cross-product magnitude of the normalized inputs and returned its asin, whose range stops at pi/2. Obtuse inputs were reflected, and +x against -x reported 0 degrees.

sections.heading: Why it was needed
sections.text: The PR's before/after table shows 120, 135 and 180 degree cases, plus the documented default argument, returning wrong values on master. Half of all angles between 0 and 180 degrees were affected, so callers received wrong results whenever two vectors were more than 90 degrees apart.

sections.heading: My contribution and the accepted change
sections.text: The two-line change in src/math.cpp computes cr = s * e beside sr and returns atan2(sr, cr) instead of asin(sr). No include was added, since atan2 comes from the math.h already included. No test file was added. The change landed on master as one commit authored by me and committed by Ltabsyy.

sections.heading: Why this approach
sections.text: Documented rationale: atan2 of the sine and cosine components is well defined across the full 0 to pi range, both values were already available in the function, and the sibling Rotate overload already pairs cr with sr, so the change brings the two into agreement.

sections.heading: Validation and outcome
sections.text: Author-reported: a local harness of hand-computed cases, two-plane sweeps, and symmetry and scale checks went from 275 failures to 0; ctest passed 14/14; ASan/UBSan Debug runs were clean. The harness was not submitted. CodeRabbit's automated review raised no actionable comments. Ltabsyy wrote "I think it's okay. Shall we merge first?" and merged on September 13, 2026.

cases.title: Correcting SHA-256 padding for edge-case lengths
cases.original_title: [rcore] Fix ComputeSHA256() wrong hash when message length mod 64 is 56..59

sections.heading: The problem
sections.text: Issue #6143 showed ComputeSHA256() returning wrong digests whenever the message length was 56 to 59 mod 64. The padding reserve used sizeof(dataSize), 4 bytes for an int, while the code below wrote a 1-byte marker and an 8-byte length, so in those cases the length overwrote the marker.

sections.heading: Why it was needed
sections.text: A hash that disagrees with FIPS 180-4 for one input length in sixteen cannot be compared with digests from other tools. The PR also noted that in the failing cases the padded buffer was one block short of the canonical size the standard requires.

sections.heading: My contribution and the accepted change
sections.text: The merged change is one line in src/rcore.c: the reserve becomes sizeof(bitLen), with a comment saying it covers the 64-bit length appended at the end. The existing round-up expression was left unchanged. The PR states that digests for the affected lengths intentionally change, because they now match the standard.

sections.heading: Why this approach
sections.text: Documented in the PR: with an 8-byte reserve, the existing round-up yields exactly the canonical size. Writing r = (dataSize + 8) mod 64, room after the message is 8 + (64 - r), at least 9 bytes, and r = 0 adds the extra block the standard requires. Keying the reserve to bitLen also matches the write loop, which already used sizeof(bitLen).

sections.heading: Validation and outcome
sections.text: Author-reported: all five NIST vectors pass, every length from 0 to 4,096 and 3,000 random messages match a reference SHA-256, padding shows 0 mismatches over 10,000,001 lengths, and ASan/UBSan runs are clean. Testing was Linux/GCC only and the harnesses stayed local, so no tests were added. raysan5 merged the PR on September 12, 2026, about three hours after it opened, without a formal review, and posted a thank-you comment.

cases.title: Diagnosing silently wrong SHA-256 digests
cases.original_title: [rcore] ComputeSHA256() returns wrong hash for messages of length 56..59 mod 64
cases.role: Bug reporter · reproducer and follow-up PR

sections.heading: The problem
sections.text: ComputeSHA256() in raylib’s rcore.c returned an incorrect hash whenever the input length was 56, 57, 58 or 59 mod 64, including the published 56-byte FIPS 180-4 two-block test vector. Every write stayed inside the allocation, so the failure produced a plausible digest instead of a crash.

sections.heading: Why it was needed
sections.text: The defect was deterministic rather than data dependent: within those four residue classes every length failed, which is 6.25% of all input lengths. With no crash or out-of-bounds access, nothing short of comparison against a reference implementation would reveal it.

sections.heading: My contribution and the resolution
sections.text: I filed the report against master at 2f768eb with a minimal program printing raylib’s digest for the FIPS vector beside the expected value, which sha256sum confirmed. I traced the cause to a 4-byte reserve, sizeof(dataSize) on an int, versus the 9 bytes of marker and 64-bit length written later. The issue was resolved by my own PR #6144.

sections.heading: Why this approach
sections.text: Sweeping lengths turned a suspected typo into a bounded defect: 256 wrong of 4,097 lengths, 210 of 3,000 random messages, and 625,000 padding mismatches up to 10,000,000, all in the same four classes. Checking SHA-1, MD5, CRC32 and Base64 against references confirmed the scope; SHA-1 already reserved the full 8 bytes.

sections.heading: Validation and outcome
sections.text: All measurements are author-reported from local harnesses that were not published; they were not re-run for this portfolio. The issue received no maintainer comment. raysan5 closed it on September 12, 2026, about three hours after filing, when the linked PR merged.

cases.title: Tokenizing scientific notation in expressions
cases.original_title: Fix scientific notation in expression tokenizer

sections.heading: The problem
sections.text: TSyntax::Tokenizer::setBuffer() scanned exponents only inside its decimal-point branch and always required s[i + 2] to be a digit. Literals such as 1.0e2, 1.0e0, 1e2 and 1e+2 were split into a Number plus further tokens, while 1.0e+2 and 1.0e02 worked.

sections.heading: Why it was needed
sections.text: The expression parser converts Number tokens into values, so a split literal is broken before evaluation, and the expression field uses the same parser for syntax highlighting. Report #7112 showed 5 of 10 inputs failing against the unchanged tokenizer.

sections.heading: My contribution and the accepted change
sections.text: The accepted change touches only ttokenizer.cpp (+9/-7). Exponent scanning moves after the optional fraction, so it applies with or without a decimal point. After e or E, an optional sign is skipped and the exponent is consumed only if a digit follows; otherwise the e is left for the identifier scanner. A token != "." guard stops a bare point acting as the mantissa.

sections.heading: Why this approach
sections.text: Documented: independent exponent scanning, an optional sign and a mandatory digit, as the report suggested. From the code: looking ahead before appending keeps malformed forms such as 1.0e+ from swallowing characters. RodneyBaker called the patch correct, minimal and well-scoped and suggested a bool instead of the "." comparison, though not as a blocker; the merged diff keeps the comparison.

sections.heading: Validation and outcome
sections.text: Author-reported: the 10-case reproducer passes; a local 34-case harness passes and fails on the original source; ASan, UBSan and LSan are clean. RodneyBaker posted a checklist (malformed exponents, 1e2+3, identifiers, .5, evaluated values) and I reported every check passing locally. No tests were committed and the GUI was not tested. RodneyBaker merged it on September 10, 2026.

cases.title: Correcting a sign in polyhedron raycasts
cases.original_title: Fix polyhedron raycasts parallel to faces

sections.heading: The problem
sections.text: shape_raycast for polyhedron_shape has a branch for segments parallel to a face. It computed dist = dot(vertex - p0, normal) and returned no hit when dist > 0, which with outward normals is the interior side of the plane. A segment through the center of a make_box_mesh() cube therefore missed.

sections.heading: Why it was needed
sections.text: Any axis-aligned segment through a box mesh is parallel to four of its faces, so the bug hit ordinary queries. Report #155 showed box_shape returning fraction 0.25 while the same cube as a polyhedron returned EDYN_SCALAR_MAX, the no-hit value, on all three axes.

sections.heading: My contribution and the accepted change
sections.text: The merged change flips one comparison in src/edyn/collision/raycast.cpp from dist > 0 to dist < 0, so only segments lying outside a parallel face's plane are rejected. The adjacent code comment already said the segment misses when it lies in front of the face; the condition now matches it. The non-parallel clipping path is untouched.

sections.heading: Why this approach
sections.text: Documented: the PR derives the sign from the outward-normal convention, where negative dist places p0 outside the face. cases.title: Coalescing free blocks during deallocation
cases.original_title: Optimize NonLocalAllocator: sorted vector + immediate coalescing

sections.heading: The problem
sections.text: NonLocalAllocator tracked free ranges using a list-shaped interface, inserted free blocks without maintaining address order, and deferred sorting and coalescing until compact(). The PR identifies extra element shifts in the default tinystl implementation and repeated merge work.

sections.heading: Why it was needed
sections.text: The allocator serves dynamic graphics buffers and the uniform cache. Repeated allocate/free activity can produce multiple neighboring free ranges, increasing entries scanned by first-fit allocation. Keeping adjacent ranges merged addresses that bookkeeping overhead while retaining the existing allocator interface.

sections.heading: My contribution and the accepted change
sections.text: Changed FreeList to stl::vector<Free>. A new insertFreeBlock uses bx::upperBound to locate the address position and checks whether the block joins the previous, next, both or neither neighbor. add and free call this helper. compact now only reports whether m_used is empty, because merging is performed during insertion. remove erases the first vector entry; Free gains operator> for the foundation library comparator.

sections.heading: Why this approach
sections.text: Documented: immediate coalescing keeps the free list compact, address ordering avoids later sort passes, and bx::upperBound follows project library conventions without introducing std containers. The body attributes the search choice to a maintainer suggestion, but no corresponding review thread is present. Binary search is O(log n); vector insertion and erasure can still move O(n) elements. First-fit allocation remains linear and now chooses the lowest-address fit.

sections.heading: Validation and outcome
sections.text: The author reports a Vulkan headless churn benchmark using 256 buffers and 2,000 measured frames, approximately 0.29 to 0.135 ms average frame time. cases.title: Batching GPU profiler queue removal
cases.original_title: perf: replace O(n²) GPUProfiler erase(0) loop with cursor + eraseRange

sections.heading: The problem
sections.text: GPUProfiler::frame() repeatedly removed the first element of m_queries while consuming ready queries. Each erase(0) moved the remaining array elements, so processing a long ready prefix could repeat substantial copying.

sections.heading: Why it was needed
sections.text: Profiling should not introduce avoidable overhead into the rendering frame it observes. With n ready queries in an array, repeated front removals can cause quadratic element movement; the operation needs only to discard one processed prefix while retaining queries not ready yet.

sections.heading: My contribution and the accepted change
sections.text: Introduced a processed cursor, read m_queries[processed], and incremented it after each successful query handling. After the loop, one guarded eraseRange(0, processed) discards the prefix. The existing early stop at the first unready query remains, as do timestamp handling, GPU block reporting, the mutex guard and returning query handles to the pool.

sections.heading: Why this approach
sections.text: Documented: batch the erasure to eliminate repeated memmoves. The source supports the inference that this preserves the queue order and readiness boundary, since only indexing and removal timing change. It reduces array compaction work without introducing a new queue container or changing callers. Linear overall work is a structural claim about processing and compaction, not a universal timing guarantee.

sections.heading: Validation and outcome
